text: Implementing Knowledge Management starts with two real tables. kb_knowledge_base is the container record — think of it as the book itself, something like a Self-Service Knowledge Base or an IT Staff Knowledge Base. kb_knowledge is each individual article, the page inside one specific book. Every article record carries a Knowledge Base reference field pointing at exactly one container, so an article always belongs to one book, never floats unassigned.

ITSM Foundations covered Knowledge Management as an ITIL practice: capture what people already know, so the next person doesn't have to re-solve the same problem. Implementing that well usually means more than one Knowledge Base. A password-reset article belongs in front of every end user. A runbook describing how to restart a production integration, with internal hostnames and escalation contacts, does not.

That's why a real instance implements a public-facing Self-Service Knowledge Base alongside an internal IT Staff Knowledge Base. It's a decision made at the container level — who can even browse this book in the first place — distinct from, and made before, any individual article's own permissions come into play.

A kb_knowledge article record carries five fields worth knowing by name: Short description, the title shown in search results; Text, the actual article body; Workflow state, which tracks Draft, Review, Published, or Retired across the next two lessons; the Knowledge Base reference, pointing at its container; and Category, a taxonomy field grouping related articles inside that one Knowledge Base, like folders inside the book.

Permissions layer the same way. Each Knowledge Base carries default Can Read and Can Contribute criteria — who may browse it, and who may author or edit pages in it — applying to every article inside as a baseline. Most articles never need more than that default. An individual article can still carry its own narrower override when it genuinely needs a tighter audience, like a security incident postmortem living inside an otherwise broadly readable IT Staff Knowledge Base.

Setting the default once at the Knowledge Base, and reserving overrides for the real exception, is what keeps permissions manageable as the article count grows into the hundreds. Next up: the real Draft, Review, Published workflow, and the approval gate that sits between Review and Published.
